1	# CoralNPU Integration Guide
2	
3	
4	
5	This document describes integrating CoralNPU as an AXI/TileLink peripheral in
6	a bigger system.
7	
8	## AXI
9	
10	We provide a scalar-only CoralNPU configuration that can integrate with an AXI
11	based system. The SystemVerilog can be generated with:
12	
13	``` bash
14	bazel build //hdl/chisel/src/coralnpu:core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog
15	```
16	
17	### Module interfaces
18	
19	![CoralNPU AXI](images/coralnpu_axi.svg)
20	
21	The interfaces to CoralNPU are defined as follows:
22	
23	|   Signal Bundle  |                   Description                             |
24	| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
25	|       clk        | The clock of the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.                     |
26	|      reset       | The active-low reset signal for the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.  |
27	|      s_axi       | An AXI4 slave interface that can be used to write TCMs or touch CoralNPU CSRs. |
28	|      m_axi       | An AXI4 master interface used by CoralNPU to read/write to memories/CSRs. |
29	|       irqn       | Active-low interrupt to the CoralNPU core. Can be triggered by peripherals or other host processor. |
30	|       wfi        | Active-high signal from the CoralNPU core, indicating that the core is waiting for an interrupt. While this is active, CoralNPU is clock-gated. |
31	|      debug       | Debug interface to monitor CoralNPU instructions execution. This interface is typically only used for simulation. |
32	|      halted      | Output interface informing if the Core is running or not. Can be ignored. |
33	|      fault       | Output interface to determine if the Core hit a fault. These signals should be connected to a system control CPU interrupt-line or status register for notification when CoralNPU faults or is halted. |
34	
35	#### AXI master signals
36	
37	AR / AW channel
38	
39	| Signal | Behaviour |
40	| ------ | --------- |
41	| addr   | Address CoralNPU wishes to read/write |
42	| prot   | Always 2 (unprivileged, insecure, data) |
43	| id     | Always 0 |
44	| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |
45	| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1, 2, or 4) |
46	| burst  | Always 1 (INCR) |
47	| lock   | Always 0 (normal access) |
48	| cache  | Always 0 (Device non-bufferable) |
49	| qos    | Always 0 |
50	| region | Always 0 |
51	
52	R channel
53	
54	| Signal | Behaviour |
55	| ------ | --------- |
56	| data   | Response data from the slave |
57	| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 |
58	| resp   | Response code |
59	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
60	
61	W channel
62	
63	| Signal | Behaviour |
64	| ------ | --------- |
65	| data   | Data CoralNPU wishes to write |
66	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
67	| strb   | Which bytes in the data are valid |
68	
69	B channel
70	
71	| Signal | Behaviour |
72	| ------ | --------- |
73	| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 (an RTL assertion exists for this) |
74	| resp   | Response code |
75	
76	Note: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.
77	
78	#### AXI slave signals
79	
80	AR / AW channel
81	
82	| Signal | Behaviour |
83	| ------ | --------- |
84	| addr   | Address the master wishes to read / write to |
85	| prot   | Ignored |
86	| id     | Transaction ID, should be reflected in the response beats |
87	| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |
88	| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1,2,4,8,16) |
89	| burst  | 0, 1, or 2 (FIXED, INCR, WRAP) |
90	| lock   | Ignored |
91	| cache  | Ignored |
92	| qos    | Ignored |
93	| region | Ignored |
94	
95	R channel
96	
97	| Signal | Behaviour |
98	| ------ | --------- |
99	| data   | Response data from CoralNPU |
100	| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AR |
101	| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR) |
102	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
103	
104	W channel
105	
106	| Signal | Behaviour |
107	| ------ | --------- |
108	| data   | Data the master wishes to write to CoralNPU |
109	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
110	| strb   | Which bytes in data are valid |
111	
112	B channel
113	
114	| Signal | Behaviour |
115	| ------ | --------- |
116	| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AW |
117	| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR)
118	
119	Note: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.
120	
121	#### Debug Signals
122	
123	| Signal   | Behaviour |
124	| -------- | --------- |
125	| en       | 4-bit value, indicating which fetch lanes are active |
126	| addr     | 32-bit values, containing the PC for each fetch lane |
127	| inst     | 32-bit values, containing the instruction for each fetch lane |
128	| cycles   | cycle counter |
129	| dbus     | Information about internal LSU transactions |
130	| -> valid | Whether the transaction is valid |
131	| -> bits  | addr: The 32-bit address for the transaction |
132	|          | write: If the transaction is a write |
133	|          | wdata: 128-bit write data for the transaction |
134	| dispatch | Information about instructions which are dispatched for execution |
135	| -> fire  | If an instruction was dispatched in the slot, this cycle |
136	| -> addr  | The 32-bit address of the instruction |
137	| -> inst  | The 32-bit value of the instruction |
138	| regfile  | Information about writes to the integer register file |
139	| -> writeAddr | Register addresses to which a future write is expected |
140	| ->-> valid | If an instruction was dispatched in this lane, which will write the regfile |
141	| ->-> bits | The 5-bit register address to which the write is expected |
142	| -> writeData | For each port in the register file, information about writes |
143	| ->-> valid | If a write occurred on this port, this cycle |
144	| ->-> bits_addr | The 5-bit register address to which the write occurred |
145	| ->-> bits_data | The 32-bit value which was written to the register |
146	| float | Information about write to the floating point register file |
147	| -> writeAddr | Register addresses to which a future write is expected |
148	| ->-> valid | If an instruction was dispatched to floating point on this cycle |
149	| ->-> bits | The address of the register to which a write is expected |
150	| -> writeData | For each port in the register file, information about writes |
151	| ->-> valid | If a write occured on this port, this cycle |
152	| ->-> bits_addr | The 5-bit register address to which the writh occurred |
153	| ->-> bits_data | The 32-bit value which was written to the register |
154	
155	
156	### CoralNPU Memory Map
157	
158	Memory accesses to CoralNPU are defined as follows:
159	
160	| Region |      Range        |  Size  | Alignment |                 Description                   |
161	| ------ | ----------------  | ------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------- |
162	|  ITCM  | 0x0000 -  0x1FFF  |   8kB  |  4 bytes  | ITCM storage for code executed by CoralNPU.     |
163	|  DTCM  | 0x10000 - 0x17FFF |  32kB  |  1 byte   | DTCM storage for data used by CoralNPU.         |
164	|  CSR   | 0x30000 - TBD     |   TBD  |  4 bytes  | CSR interface used to query/control CoralNPU.   |
165	
166	### Reset Considerations
167	CoralNPU uses a synchronous reset strategy -- to ensure proper reset behavior, ensure that the clock runs for a cycle with reset active, before enabling either the internal clock gate (via CSR) or gating externally.
168	
169	## Booting CoralNPU
170	A note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.
171	
172	1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.
173	```c
174	volatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;
175	for (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {
176	    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];
177	}
178	```
179	
180	If something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.
181	
182	2. Program the start PC
183	If your program is linked such that the starting address is 0, you may skip this.
184	
185	```c
186	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_pc_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030004L;
187	*coralnpu_pc_csr = start_addr;
188	```
189	
190	3. Release clock gate
191	```c
192	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;
193	*coralnpu_reset_csr = 1;
194	```
195	
196	After this, ensure you wait a cycle to allow CoralNPU's reset to occur.
197	If you want to configure something like an interrupt that is connected to CoralNPU's
198	fault or halted outputs, this is a good time.
199	
200	4. Release reset
201	```c
202	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;
203	*coralnpu_reset_csr = 0;
204	```
205	
206	At this point, CoralNPU will begin executing at the PC programmed in step 2.
207	
208	5. Monitor for `io_halted`
209	The status of CoralNPU's execution can be checked by reading the status CSR:
210	```c
211	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_status_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030008L;
212	uint32_t status = *coralnpu_status_csr;
213	bool halted = status & 1;
214	bool fault = status & 2;
215	```
216	
217	# CoralNPU CSRs
218	Note: These are CSRs that are intended to be read or written externally
219	to CoralNPU, e.g. by the host processor in a system.
220	They are not the same as the RISC-V CSRs accessed via the Zicsr ISA extension.
221	
222	### Register: `RESET_CONTROL`
223	*   **Offset**: `0x0`
224	*   **Description**: Controls reset and clock gating for the CoralNPU core. On power-up, the core is held in reset with its clock gated. To start the core, the clock gate should be released first, followed by de-asserting reset.
225	
226	| Bits  | Name         | Description                                                                                             | Access | Reset Value |
227	| :---- | :----------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :----- | :---------- |
228	| 0     | `RESET`      | When 1, the core is held in reset. When 0, the core is not in reset.                                    | R/W    | 1           |
229	| 1     | `CLOCK_GATE` | When 1, the core's clock is gated. When 0, the core's clock is running.                                 | R/W    | 1           |
230	| 31:2  | `RESERVED`   | Reserved, writes ignored, reads return 0.                                                               | R      | 0           |
231	
232	### Register: `PC_START`
233	*   **Offset**: `0x4`
234	*   **Description**: Sets the program counter for the CoralNPU core. This should be programmed before releasing the core from reset.
235	
236	| Bits  | Name            | Description                                         | Access | Reset Value |
237	| :---- | :-------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- | :----- | :---------- |
238	| 31:0  | `START_ADDRESS` | The address where the core will begin execution.    | R/W    | 0           |
239	
240	### Register: `STATUS`
241	*   **Offset**: `0x8`
242	*   **Description**: Provides status on the CoralNPU core. This is a read-only register.
243	
244	| Bits  | Name       | Description                                                              | Access | Reset Value |
245	| :---- | :--------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----- | :---------- |
246	| 0     | `HALTED`   | When 1, the core has halted (e.g. after an `mpause` instruction).        | R      | 0           |
247	| 1     | `FAULT`    | When 1, the core has encountered a fault.                                | R      | 0           |
248	| 31:2  | `RESERVED` | Reserved, reads return 0.                                                | R      | 0           |
249

1	# CoralNPU
2	
3	CoralNPU is a RISCV CPU built with custom SIMD instructions and microarchitectural
4	decisions that align with the dataplane properties of an ML accelerator. The design
5	of CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar
6	capabilities are then added for a fused design.
7	
8	## Block Diagram
9	
10	![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)
11	
12	## Scalar Core
13	
14	A simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD
15	backend.
16	
17	CoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of
18	instructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no
19	interrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension
20	encoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary
21	encoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type
22	encodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction
23	set. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.
24	
25	The branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward
26	branches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not
27	match the decision in the fetch unit.
28	
29	Registers        | Names         | Width
30	---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------
31	Scalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits
32	Control & Status | CSRx          | Various
33	
34	## Vector Core
35	
36	We use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD
37	instruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend
38	is decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector
39	instructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are
40	resolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.
41	
42	Registers        | Names         | Width
43	---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------
44	Vector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)
45	Accumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits
46	
47	
48	### MAC
49	
50	The central component of the design is a quantized outer product
51	multiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional
52	broadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect
53	to memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution
54	weights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches
55	(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).
56	
57	![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)
58	
59	The outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT
60	opcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and
61	performing 256 MACs per cycle.
62	
63	### Stripmining
64	
65	Strip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available
66	hardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming
67	a bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through
68	the SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a
69	stripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the
70	command queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For
71	instance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :
72	vadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.
73	
74	## Cache
75	
76	Caches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared
77	SRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the
78	backend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.
79	
80	The L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.
81	
82	The L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop
83	management and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set
84	associativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank
85	architecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows
86	for a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment
87	buffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to
88	simplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of
89	the memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external
90	memory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core
91	stalls until completion to simplify the contract.
92

1	# Coral NPU
2	
3	Coral NPU is a hardware accelerator for ML inferencing. Coral NPU is an Open Source IP designed by Google Research and is freely available for integration into ultra-low-power System-on-Chips (SoCs) targeting wearable devices such as hearables, augmented reality (AR) glasses and smart watches.
4	
5	Coral NPU is a neural processing unit (NPU), also known as an AI accelerator or deep-learning processor. Coral NPU is based on the 32-bit RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).
6	
7	Coral NPU includes three distinct processor components that work together: matrix, vector (SIMD), and scalar.
8	
9	![Coral NPU Archicture](doc/images/arch_data_flow.png)
10	[Coral NPU Architecture Datasheet](https://developers.google.com/coral/guides/hardware/datasheet)
11	
12	## Coral NPU Features
13	Coral NPU offers the following top-level feature set:
14	
15	* RV32IMF_Zve32x RISC-V instruction set (specifically `rv32imf_zve32x_zicsr_zifencei_zbb`)
16	* 32-bit address space for applications and operating system kernels
17	* Four-stage processor, in-order dispatch, out-of-order retire
18	* Four-way scalar, two-way vector dispatch
19	* 128-bit SIMD, 256-bit (future) pipeline
20	* 8 KB ITCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for instructions)
21	* 32 KB DTCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for data)
22	* Both memories are single-cycle-latency SRAM, more efficient than cache memory
23	* AXI4 bus interfaces, functioning as both manager and subordinate, to interact with external memory and allow external CPUs to configure Coral NPU
24	
25	## System Requirements
26	
27	* Bazel 7.4.1
28	* Python 3.9-3.12 (3.13 support is in progress)
29	* [SRecord](https://srecord.sourceforge.net/)
30	
31	## Quick Start
32	
33	```bash
34	# Ensure that test suite passes
35	bazel run //tests/cocotb:core_mini_axi_sim_cocotb
36	
37	# Build a binary
38	bazel build //examples:coralnpu_v2_hello_world_add_floats
39	
40	# Build the Simulator (non-RVV for shorter build time):
41	bazel build //tests/verilator_sim:core_mini_axi_sim
42	
43	# Run the binary on the simulator:
44	bazel-bin/tests/verilator_sim/core_mini_axi_sim --binary bazel-out/k8-fastbuild-ST-dd8dc713f32d/bin/examples/coralnpu_v2_hello_world_add_floats.elf
45	```
46

20	class FpuSpec extends AnyFreeSpec with ChiselSim {
21	  def Float2Bits(x: Float): (Boolean, Int, Int) = {
22	    val abs = x.abs
23	    val int = java.lang.Float.floatToIntBits(abs)
24	
25	    val sign: Boolean = (x < 0)
26	    val exponent: Int = int >> 23
27	    val mantissa: Int = int & ((1 << 23) - 1)
28	
29	    (sign, exponent, mantissa)
30	  }
31	
32	  def EnqueueValid(fpu: Fpu, op: FpuOptype.Type, ina: Float, inb: Float, inc: Float, waddr: Int) = {
33	    fpu.io.cmd.valid.poke(1)
34	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.optype.poke(op)
35	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.waddr.poke(waddr)
36	
37	    val ina_bits = Float2Bits(ina)
38	    val inb_bits = Float2Bits(inb)
39	    val inc_bits = Float2Bits(inc)
40	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.ina.sign.poke(ina_bits._1)
41	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.ina.exponent.poke(ina_bits._2)
42	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.ina.mantissa.poke(ina_bits._3)
43	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inb.sign.poke(inb_bits._1)
44	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inb.exponent.poke(inb_bits._2)
45	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inb.mantissa.poke(inb_bits._3)
46	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inc.sign.poke(inc_bits._1)
47	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inc.exponent.poke(inc_bits._2)
48	    fpu.io.cmd.bits.inc.mantissa.poke(inc_bits._3)
49	  }
50	
51	  def GetFloat(fpu: Fpu): Float = {
52	    val sign = fpu.io.output.bits.bits.sign.peek().litValue
53	    val exponent = fpu.io.output.bits.bits.exponent.peek().litValue
54	    val mantissa = fpu.io.output.bits.bits.mantissa.peek().litValue
55	    val int_val = ((exponent << 23) + mantissa).toInt
56	    val negate = if (sign == 1) -1.0f else 1.0f
57	
58	    negate * java.lang.Float.intBitsToFloat(int_val)
59	  }
60	
61	  "Pipeline" in {
62	    simulate(new Fpu) { dut =>
63	      dut.io.output.ready.poke(1)
64	      EnqueueValid(dut, FpuOptype.FpuAdd, 1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f, 1)
65	      dut.clock.step()
66	      EnqueueValid(dut, FpuOptype.FpuSub, 1.0f, 0.0f, -1.0f, 2)
67	      dut.clock.step()
68	
69	      dut.io.output.valid.expect(1)
70	      dut.io.output.bits.addr.expect(1)
71	      assertResult(2.0f) { GetFloat(dut) }
72	      EnqueueValid(dut, FpuOptype.FpuMul, 1.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f, 3)
73	      dut.clock.step()
74	
75	      dut.io.output.valid.expect(1)
76	      dut.io.output.bits.addr.expect(2)
77	      assertResult(2.0f) { GetFloat(dut) }
78	      dut.io.cmd.valid.poke(0)
79	      dut.clock.step()
80	
81	
82	      dut.io.output.valid.expect(1)
83	      dut.io.output.bits.addr.expect(3)
84	      assertResult(1.0f) { GetFloat(dut) }
85	      dut.clock.step()
86	
87	      dut.io.output.valid.expect(0)
88	    }
89	  }

25	  def rotateLeft(num: BigInt, shift: Int, width: Int): BigInt = {
26	    val effectiveShift = shift % width // Handle shifts larger than width
27	    val leftPart = (num << effectiveShift) & ((BigInt(1) << width) - 1)
28	    val rightPart = num >> (width - effectiveShift)
29	    leftPart | rightPart
30	  }
31	
32	  def generateMasks(addr: Int, size: Int, txnSizes: Seq[Int]): List[BigInt] = {
33	    val bottom: Int = addr & 0x1F
34	    val mask0 = rotateLeft((31 to 0 by -1).map(i => i < txnSizes(0)).foldLeft(0L) { (acc, b) => (acc << 1 | (if (b) 1L else 0L))}, bottom, 32)
35	    val mask1 = rotateLeft((31 to 0 by -1).map(i => i < txnSizes(1)).foldLeft(0L) { (acc, b) => (acc << 1 | (if (b) 1L else 0L))}, bottom + txnSizes(0), 32)
36	    List(mask0, mask1)
37	  }
38	
39	  def generateBitmask(bytemask: BigInt): BigInt = {
40	    var bitmask: BigInt = 0
41	    for (i <- 31 to 0 by -1) {
42	      bitmask = (bitmask | (if (bytemask.testBit(i)) 255 else 0)) << 8
43	    }
44	    bitmask >>= 8
45	    bitmask
46	  }

182	        dut.io.dbus.size.poke(c.size.U)
183	        dut.clock.step()
184	
185	        val (len, addr, size) = {
186	          assertResult(0) { dut.io.axi.read.addr.ready.peek().litValue }
187	          dut.io.axi.read.addr.ready.poke(true.B)
188	          while (dut.io.axi.read.addr.valid.peek().litValue != 1 || dut.io.axi.read.addr.ready.peek().litValue != 1) {
189	            dut.clock.step()
190	          }
191	          val rv = (
192	            dut.io.axi.read.addr.bits.len.peek().litValue,
193	            dut.io.axi.read.addr.bits.addr.peek().litValue,
194	            dut.io.axi.read.addr.bits.size.peek().litValue,
195	          )
196	          dut.clock.step()
197	          dut.io.axi.read.addr.ready.poke(false.B)
198	          rv
199	        }
200	
201	        assertResult(len) { 0 }
202	        assertResult(size) { log2Ceil(c.size) }
203	        assertResult(addr) { c.addr }
204	
205	        {
206	          assertResult(0) { dut.io.axi.read.data.valid.peek().litValue }
207	          for (i <- 0 to (len).toInt) {
208	            dut.io.axi.read.data.valid.poke(true)
209	            dut.io.axi.read.data.bits.id.poke(0)
210	            dut.io.axi.read.data.bits.data.poke(0)
211	            dut.io.axi.read.data.bits.resp.poke(0) // OKAY
212	            dut.io.axi.read.data.bits.last.poke(true)
213	            assertResult(1) { dut.io.dbus.ready.peek().litValue }
214	            dut.clock.step()
215	            while (dut.io.axi.read.data.valid.peek().litValue != 1 || dut.io.axi.read.data.ready.peek().litValue != 1) {
216	              dut.clock.step()
217	            }
218	            dut.io.dbus.valid.poke(false.B)
219	            dut.io.axi.read.data.valid.poke(false.B)
220	            dut.clock.step()
221	          }
222	          dut.io.axi.read.data.valid.poke(false.B)
223	          dut.clock.step()
224	        }
225	      })
226	    }

1	# CoralNPU Microarchitecture
2	
3	![image](../images/microarch.png)
4	
5	## Pipeline
6	
7	The CoralNPU base processor is an in-order three-stage pipeline capable of
8	dispatching up to 4 instructions per cycle. The instruction stages are:
9	
10	* **Instruction fetch:** Instructions are fetched from memory into an
11	instruction buffer.
12	* **Decode/Dispatch:** The first 4 instructions in the instruction buffer are
13	decoded. Interlock and scoreboard logic determine which of the instructions can
14	be dispatched this cycle. Instructions are forwarded to their respective
15	execution units.
16	* **Execute/Writeback:** Execution units with dispatched instructions read
17	operands from the register file and perform computation. Results can also be
18	written back to the register file in the same cycle.
19	
20	Some execution units can take multiple cycles to execute. Instruction latencies
21	can be found in the table below:
22	
23	| Instruction Type | Latency (cycles) | Description            |
24	| ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
25	| Alu              | 1                | Add, sub, xor, ...     |
26	| Csr              | 1                | CSR instructions       |
27	| Bru              | 1                | bge, jal, ebreak, ...  |
28	| Mlu              | 2                | mul, mulh, ...         |
29	| Dvu              | Variable         | div, rem, ...          |
30	| Lsu              | 2+               | lw, sw, ...            |

1	# Multiplication Unit
2	
3	The Multiply Unit (MLU) executes multiplication operations: MUL, MULH, MULHSU
4	and MULHU.
5	
6	## Interfaces
7	
8	Inputs to the MLU are instructions from the Dispatch Unit or data reads from the
9	Register File. The single MLU in the CoralNPU core can service instructions from
10	any of the four instruction lanes, but only one command is dispatched in any
11	cycle.
12	
13	Outputs of the MLU are writes to the Register file.
14	
15	Figure 1 shows the inputs and outputs to and from the MLU.
16	
17	![image](../images/mlu_interfaces.png)
18	
19	Figure 1: Mlu interfaces
20	
21	### MLU Inputs
22	
23	Note: There are 4 instances of each of these signals (one for each instruction
24	lane).
25	
26	| Signal Name  | Type          | Description                                                        |
27	| ------------ | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
28	| req.valid    | Bool          | If the command if valid.                                           |
29	| req.op       |               | The function to execute.                                           |
30	| req.addr     | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to.                        |
31	| req.ready    | Bool (output) | If the command is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake.      |
32	| rs1.valid    | Bool          | If there is a valid rs1 read this cycle. Only used for assertions. |
33	| rs1.data     | UInt(32)      | The rs1 data read from the RegFile.                                |
34	| rs2.valid    | Bool          | If there is a valid rs1 read this cycle. Only used for assertions. |
35	| rs2.data     | UInt(32)      | The rs2 data read from the RegFile.                                |
36	
37	### MLU Outputs
38	
39	| Signal Name | Type     | Description                                                                       |
40	| ----------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
41	| rd.valid    | Bool     | If the command if valid.                                                          |
42	| rd.addr     | UInt(5)  | The RegFile address to write the result to.                                       |
43	| rd.data     | UInt(32) | The computation result to write to RegFile.                                       |
44	| rd.ready    | Bool     | If the write result is accepted by the RegFile. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
45	
46	### Timing/Pipeline
47	
48	The MLU is a three stage pipeline, with the following stages:
49	
50	1. **Dispatch:** The dispatch unit determines if MLU operations can be executed.
51	Amongst the four lanes, the MLU accepts the first valid MLU instruction. This
52	request will be processed next cycle.
53	2. **Compute:** The second stage performs computation of the multiplication,
54	using the register read data from rs1 and rs2.
55	2. **Writeback:** The multiplication result is stored back to the register file.
56	
57	A waveform showing a typical interaction with the waveform can be found in
58	Figure 2:
59	
60	![image](../images/mlu_waveform.png)
61	
62	Figure 2: Mlu waveform.
63

1	# Load Store Unit
2	
3	![image](../images/lsu.svg)
4	
5	The Load Store Unit handles memory operations issued by the core. Functionally,
6	it's purpose is to translate memory instructions into transactions on the
7	appropriate subsystem.
8	
9	## Slots
10	
11	The CoralNPU LSU uses a concept called _slots_ to handle memory transactions. A
12	slot is a data structure which manages the state of a single dispatched LSU
13	operation and determines what memory transaction should be performed. At its
14	core, there exists a table in each slot which tracks which part of the memory
15	operation has been completed.
16	
17	For example, below is the slot table for a word-store into address 0xDEADBEEF:
18	
19	| Index | Active |   Address  | Data |
20	| ----- | ------ | ---------- | ---- |
21	|   0   |    1   | 0xDEADBEEF | 0x01 |
22	|   1   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF0 | 0x23 |
23	|   2   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF1 | 0x45 |
24	|   3   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF2 | 0x67 |
25	|   4   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |
26	...
27	|   n   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |
28	
29	Memory transactions over TCM or AXI busses will read/write data in the slot
30	table and flip the active bits to 0 as they are made.
31	
32	The typical lifetime of a slot is as follows:
33	
34	1) **Idle**: An idle slot will dequeue a LsuOperation from the command queue.
35	Scalar operations will move directly into **Transfer Memory** while vector
36	operations will go to the **Vector Update** state.
37	2) **Vector Update**: For vector operations masks, addresses (for indexed ops)
38	and data (for store ops) need to be received from the RvvCore. This stage is
39	bypassed for scalar operations.
40	3) **Transfer Memory**: While there are still active entries in the slot table,
41	the active entry with the lowest "index" will be selected for a memory
42	transaction. A scatter/gather unit will then select all other active entries
43	(although not necessarily contiguous) that will be bundled with the transaction.
44	The appropriate memory bus (ibus, dbus, ebus) will then be selected and a memory
45	transaction will be conducted. When there are no active entries, the slot moves
46	into the next state (**Writeback**).
47	4) **Writeback**: Once all memory transactions are completed, the result must
48	be written back to register files. Additionally, vector stores are
49	"acknowledged" back to the RvvCore. Scalar and floating point scores bypass this
50	stage. Once writeback is completed, the slot moves back into the
51	**Vector Update** state for LMUL > 1, or the **Idle** state.
52	
53	CoralNPU currently uses one "slot" in the LSU. In the future, multiple slots maybe
54	added to allow multiple operations to partake in the same transaction.
55	
56	## Interfaces
57	
58	### LSU Command Interface
59	
60	The LSU has a command interface coming from the dispatch unit and register file.
61	
62	| Signal Name   | Type          | Description                                                   |
63	| ------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
64	| req.valid     | Bool          | If the LSU command is valid.                                  |
65	| req.op        |               | The LSU operation to execute.                                 |
66	| req.addr      | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to for loads.         |
67	| req.pc        | UInt(32)      | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.       |
68	| req.elemWidth | UInt(32)      | Used in the RVV only. The EEW for strided loads.              |
69	| req.ready     | Bool (output) | If the command is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
70	
71	### Bus Interfaces
72	
73	| Signal Name | Type              | Description                                                       |
74	| ----------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
75	| ibus.valid  | Bool              | If the ibus transaction is valid.                                 |
76	| ibus.addr   | UInt(32)          | The address of the ibus transaction.                              |
77	| ibus.rdata  | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the ibus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
78	| ibus.ready  | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
79	
80	| Signal Name | Type              | Description                                                       |
81	| ----------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
82	| dbus.valid  | Bool              | If the dbus transaction is valid.                                 |
83	| dbus.addr   | UInt(32)          | The address of the dbus transaction.                              |
84	| dbus.size   | UInt(5)           | The size of this transaction in bytes.                            |
85	| dbus.pc     | UInt(32)          | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.           |
86	| dbus.rdata  | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the dbus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
87	| dbus.wdata  | UInt(128)         | The data to write from the dbus.                                  |
88	| dbus.wmask  | UInt(16)          | A byte write mask for this transaction.                           |
89	| dbus.ready  | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
90	
91	| Signal Name      | Type              | Description                                                       |
92	| ---------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
93	| ebus.valid       | Bool              | If the ebus transaction is valid.                                 |
94	| ebus.addr        | UInt(32)          | The address of the ebus transaction.                              |
95	| ebus.size        | UInt(5)           | The size of this transaction in bytes.                            |
96	| ebus.pc          | UInt(32)          | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.           |
97	| ebus.rdata       | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the ebus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
98	| ebus.wdata       | UInt(128)         | The data to write from the ebus.                                  |
99	| ebus.wmask       | UInt(16)          | A byte write mask for this transaction.                           |
100	| ebus.ready       | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
101	| ebus.fault.valid | Bool (input)      | Raised if a fault occurs on the external bus.                     |
102	| ebus.fault.write | Bool (input)      | If the fault occured on a write operation.                        |
103	| ebus.fault.addr  | Bool (input)      | The address of the memory transaction when the fault occurred.    |
104	| ebus.fault.epc   | Bool (input)      | The PC of the instruction that triggered the fault.               |
105	| ebus.internal    | Bool              | Not used.                                                         |
106	
107	### Writeback Interfaces
108	
109	| Signal Name | Type     | Description                                              |
110	| ----------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
111	| rd.valid    | Bool     | If the writeback to the scalar regfile is valid.         |
112	| rd.addr     | UInt(5)  | The address of the scalar register file to writeback to. |
113	| rd.data     | UInt(32) | The data to write to the scalar register file.           |
114	
115	| Signal Name     | Type     | Description                                                      |
116	| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
117	| rd_flt.valid    | Bool     | If the writeback to the floating point regfile is valid.         |
118	| rd_flt.addr     | UInt(5)  | The address of the floating point register file to writeback to. |
119	| rd_flt.data     | UInt(32) | The data to write to the floating point register file.           |
120	
121	### RVV Interfaces
122	
123	For the RVVCore, the LSU contains the following interfaces:
124	
125	| Signal Name            | Type              | Description                                                       |
126	| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
127	| rvv2lsu.valid          | Bool              | If the rvv2lsu transaction is valid.                              |
128	| rvv2lsu.idx.valid      | Bool              | If there is valid index data from the vector register file.       |
129	| rvv2lsu.idx.addr       | UInt(5)           | The address of the indices from the vector register file.         |
130	| rvv2lsu.idx.data       | UInt(128)         | The indices from the vector register file index.                  |
131	| rvv2lsu.vregfile.valid | UInt(128)         | If there is valid data from the vector register file.             |
132	| rvv2lsu.vregfile.addr  | UInt(5)           | The address of the data from the vector register file.            |
133	| rvv2lsu.vregfile.data  | UInt(128)         | The vector data to write back for this operation.                 |
134	| rvv2lsu.mask           | UInt(16)          | A byte activity mask for this transaction.                        |
135	| rvv2lsu.ready          | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
136	
137	| Signal Name    | Type              | Description                                                       |
138	| -------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
139	| lsu2rvv.valid  | Bool              | If the lsu2rvv transaction is valid.                              |
140	| lsu2rvv.addr   | UInt(5)           | The destination vector register file index.                       |
141	| lsu2rvv.data   | UInt(128)         | The vector data to write back for load operations.                |
142	| lsu2rvv.last   | Bool              | If this transaction is a store or not.                            |
143	| lsu2rvv.ready  | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
144

21	/** Helper trait for TileLink-UL test transactions. */
22	trait TLULTestUtils extends ChiselSim { this: TestSuite =>
23	
24	  /** Helper to perform a TileLink Put transaction. */
25	  def tlWrite(
26	      tl: OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device,
27	      clock: Clock,
28	      addr: UInt,
29	      data: UInt,
30	      mask: UInt = 0xf.U,
31	      size: UInt = 2.U,
32	      source: UInt = 0.U
33	  ): Unit = {
34	    tl.a.valid.poke(true.B)
35	    tl.a.bits.opcode.poke(TLULOpcodesA.PutFullData.asUInt)
36	    tl.a.bits.address.poke(addr)
37	    tl.a.bits.data.poke(data)
38	    tl.a.bits.mask.poke(mask)
39	    tl.a.bits.size.poke(size)
40	    tl.a.bits.source.poke(source)
41	    while (tl.a.ready.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
42	    clock.step()
43	    tl.a.valid.poke(false.B)
44	    while (tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
45	    tl.d.ready.poke(true.B)
46	    clock.step()
47	    tl.d.ready.poke(false.B)
48	  }
49	
50	  /** Helper to perform a TileLink Get transaction. Returns (data, error). */
51	  def tlRead(
52	      tl: OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device,
53	      clock: Clock,
54	      addr: UInt,
55	      size: UInt = 2.U,
56	      source: UInt = 0.U
57	  ): (BigInt, Boolean) = {
58	    tl.a.valid.poke(true.B)
59	    tl.a.bits.opcode.poke(TLULOpcodesA.Get.asUInt)
60	    tl.a.bits.address.poke(addr)
61	    tl.a.bits.size.poke(size)
62	    tl.a.bits.source.poke(source)
63	    while (tl.a.ready.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
64	    clock.step()
65	    tl.a.valid.poke(false.B)
66	    while (tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
67	    val data  = tl.d.bits.data.peek().litValue
68	    val error = tl.d.bits.error.peek().litValue != 0
69	    tl.d.ready.poke(true.B)
70	    clock.step()
71	    tl.d.ready.poke(false.B)
72	    (data, error)
73	  }
74	
75	  /** Wrapper for tlRead to maintain compatibility with existing tests that only expect data. */
76	  def tlReadData(
77	      tl: OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device,
78	      clock: Clock,
79	      addr: UInt,
80	      size: UInt = 2.U,
81	      source: UInt = 0.U
82	  ): BigInt = {
83	    tlRead(tl, clock, addr, size, source)._1
84	  }
85	}

29	  val count = RegInit(0.U(32.W))
30	  val limit = RegInit(256.U(32.W))
31	  val enable = RegInit(0.U(32.W))  // Counts if non-zero
32	
33	  val readMap = Map.apply(
34	      "count" -> (0, count),
35	      "limit" -> (4, limit),
36	      "enable" -> (8, enable),
37	  )
38	  io.axi.read <> ConnectAxiRead(6, readMap)
39	
40	  val writeMap = Map.apply(
41	      "count" -> 0,
42	      "limit" -> 4,
43	      "enable" -> 8,
44	  )
45	  val (writes, writeData) = ConnectAxiWrite(6, writeMap, io.axi.write)
46	
47	  val hasWrite = Wire(Bool())
48	  val axiWriteAddr = Wire(UInt(32.W))
49	  val axiWriteData = Wire(UInt(32.W))
50	  hasWrite := false.B
51	  axiWriteAddr := 0.U
52	  axiWriteData := 0.U
53	
54	  val increment = enable =/= 0.U
55	  val incCount = count + increment
56	  val overflowCount = Mux(incCount >= limit, 0.U, incCount)
57	  count := Mux(writes("count"), writeData, overflowCount)
58	
59	  when (writes("limit")) {
60	    limit := writeData
61	  }
62	
63	  when (writes("enable")) {
64	    enable := writeData
65	  }
66

51	      dut.io.dataOut(0).expect(5)

56	  "Write n" in {
57	    simulate(new CircularBufferMulti(UInt(32.W), 4, 16)) { dut =>
58	      dut.io.nEnqueued.expect(0)

62	        dut.io.enqData(n).poke(n)

69	      for (n <- 0 until 4) {
70	        dut.io.dataOut(n).expect(n)
71	      }
72	    }

76	    simulate(new CircularBufferMulti(UInt(32.W), 4, 16)) { dut =>
77	      dut.io.nEnqueued.expect(0)
78	      dut.io.flush.poke(false)
79

96	      dut.io.nEnqueued.expect(0)
97	      dut.io.flush.poke(false)
98

126	      dut.io.nEnqueued.expect(0)
127	      dut.io.flush.poke(false)

207	        }
208	        dut.io.enqValid.poke(4)

32	  def csrWrite(tl: OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device, clock: Clock, addr: UInt, data: UInt): Unit = {
33	    tl.a.valid.poke(true.B)
34	    tl.a.bits.opcode.poke(TLULOpcodesA.PutFullData.asUInt)
35	    tl.a.bits.address.poke(addr)
36	    tl.a.bits.data.poke(data)
37	    tl.a.bits.mask.poke(0xf.U)
38	    while (tl.a.ready.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
39	    clock.step()
40	    tl.a.valid.poke(false.B)
41	    while (tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
42	    tl.d.ready.poke(true.B)
43	    clock.step()
44	    tl.d.ready.poke(false.B)
45	  }
46	
47	  def csrRead(tl: OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device, clock: Clock, addr: UInt): (BigInt, Boolean) = {
48	    tl.a.valid.poke(true.B)
49	    tl.a.bits.opcode.poke(TLULOpcodesA.Get.asUInt)
50	    tl.a.bits.address.poke(addr)
51	    while (tl.a.ready.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
52	    clock.step()
53	    tl.a.valid.poke(false.B)
54	    while (tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 0) clock.step()
55	    val data  = tl.d.bits.data.peek().litValue
56	    val error = tl.d.bits.error.peek().litValue != 0
57	    tl.d.ready.poke(true.B)
58	    clock.step()
59	    tl.d.ready.poke(false.B)
60	    (data, error)
61	  }

57	      tlWrite(dut.io.tl, dut.clock, 0x10.U, testData.U, 0xffff.U, 4.U, 1.U)

61	      val rdata = tlReadData(dut.io.tl, dut.clock, 0x10.U, 4.U, 2.U)
62	      assert(rdata == testData, s"Expected 0x${testData.toString(16)}, got 0x${rdata.toString(16)}")

66	      tlWrite(dut.io.tl, dut.clock, 0x20.U, testData2.U, 0xffff.U, 4.U, 1.U)
67	      val rdata2 = tlReadData(dut.io.tl, dut.clock, 0x20.U, 4.U, 2.U)

72	  "TlulToSram should handle backpressure" in {
73	    simulate(new Module {
74	      val io = IO(new Bundle {
75	        val tl = Flipped(new OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device(tlul_p))
76	      })
77	      val dut = Module(new TlulToSram(p, 10))
78	      io.tl <> dut.io.tl

80	      // Mock SRAM
81	      val rvalid = RegInit(false.B)
82	      val rdata  = RegInit(0.U(128.W))
83	      dut.io.sram.rvalid := rvalid
84	      dut.io.sram.rdata  := rdata
85	      rvalid             := dut.io.sram.enable
86	    }) { dut =>
87	      dut.reset.poke(true.B)
88	      dut.clock.step()
89	      dut.reset.poke(false.B)
90	
91	      // Stall the D channel
92	      dut.io.tl.d.ready.poke(false.B)
93	
94	      // Send a request
95	      dut.io.tl.a.valid.poke(true.B)
96	      dut.io.tl.a.bits.opcode.poke(TLULOpcodesA.Get.asUInt)
97	      dut.io.tl.a.bits.address.poke(0x10.U)
98	
99	      while (dut.io.tl.a.ready.peek().litValue == 0) dut.clock.step()
100	      dut.clock.step()
101	      dut.io.tl.a.valid.poke(false.B)
102	
103	      // Request should be in the pipeline, but D channel is stalled.
104	      // Wait a few cycles.
105	      dut.clock.step(5)
106	
107	      // D channel should have a valid response waiting
108	      assert(dut.io.tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 1)
109	
110	      // Now release the stall
111	      dut.io.tl.d.ready.poke(true.B)
112	      dut.clock.step()
113	      assert(dut.io.tl.d.valid.peek().litValue == 0)
114	    }

62	  // safe=true is recommended to prevent metastability issues when the queue

81	      val deqValidTimeoutCycles = 50
82	
83	      // Initialize inputs

91	      dut.clock.step(initialDelayCycles)
92	
93	      // Enqueue an item
94	      dut.io.enq.valid.poke(true.B)
95	      dut.io.enq.bits.poke(123.U)
96	      dut.io.enq.ready.expect(true.B) // Should be ready immediately after reset
97	      // Hold valid for enough cycles to guarantee a rising edge on the slower enq_clock
98	      dut.clock.step(enqHoldCycles)
99	      dut.io.enq.valid.poke(false.B)
100	
101	      // Wait for deq.valid to go high, with a timeout
102	      var timeout = deqValidTimeoutCycles
103	      while (!dut.io.deq.valid.peek().litToBoolean && timeout > 0) {
104	        dut.clock.step()
105	        timeout -= 1
106	      }
107	      if (timeout == 0) {
108	        fail(s"Timed out after ${deqValidTimeoutCycles} cycles waiting for deq.valid to go high")
109	      }
110	
111	      // Dequeue the item
112	      dut.io.deq.ready.poke(true.B)
113	      dut.io.deq.valid.expect(true.B)
114	      dut.io.deq.bits.expect(123.U)
115	      dut.clock.step()
116	    }

19	/** Effectively "reinterpret_casts" a float32 into a BigInt. BigInt is used
20	  * because there's no easy uint32 type in scala, but BigInt works well enough
21	  * for Chisel use cases.
22	  * @param f A scala float.
23	  * @return A BigInt (representing uint32) bit interpretation of the float.
24	  */
25	object Float2BigInt {
26	  def apply(f: Float): BigInt = {
27	    val abs = f.abs
28	    var int = BigInt(java.lang.Float.floatToIntBits(abs))
29	    if (f < 0) {
30	      int += (BigInt(1) << 31)
31	    }
32	    int
33	  }
34	}
35	
36	/** Breaks down a float32 into it's sign, exponent and mantissa.
37	  * @param f A scala float.
38	  * @return A tuple of the sign, exponent and mantissa.
39	  */
40	object Float2Bits {
41	  def apply(f: Float): (Boolean, Int, Int) = {
42	    val abs = f.abs
43	    val int = java.lang.Float.floatToIntBits(abs)
44	
45	    val sign: Boolean = (f < 0)
46	    val exponent: Int = int >> 23
47	    val mantissa: Int = int & ((1 << 23) - 1)
48	
49	    (sign, exponent, mantissa)
50	  }
51	}
52	
53	/** Pokes a float.
54	  * @param dut The float input.
55	  * @param f A scala float.
56	  */
57	object PokeFloat {
58	  def apply(dut: Fp32, f: Float) = {
59	    val int = java.lang.Float.floatToRawIntBits(f)
60	    val sign = if (int < 0) { true.B } else { false.B }
61	    val mantissa = int & 0x7FFFFF
62	    val exponent = (int >> 23) & 0xFF
63	
64	    dut.sign := sign
65	    dut.mantissa := mantissa.U
66	    dut.exponent := exponent.U
67	  }
68	}
69	
70	/** Peeks a float.
71	  * @param dut The float input.
72	  * @param f A scala float.
73	  */
74	object PeekFloat {
75	  def apply(sign: Int, exponent: Int, mantissa: Int): Float = {
76	    val i = (sign << 31) + (exponent << 23) + mantissa
77	    java.lang.Float.intBitsToFloat(i.toInt)
78	  }
79	}

22	class FIFOStateTestWrapper(t: UInt, n: Int, capacity: Int) extends Module {
23	  val io = IO(new Bundle {
24	    val enqValid = Input(UInt(log2Ceil(n+1).W))
25	    val enqData = Input(Vec(n, t))
26	    val deqReady = Input(UInt(log2Ceil(n+1).W))
27	    val flush = Input(Bool())
28	
29	    val nEnqueued = Output(UInt(log2Ceil(capacity+1).W))
30	    val dataOut = Output(Vec(n, t))
31	  })
32	
33	  val state = RegInit(FIFOState.init(capacity, t))
34	
35	  // Chain: Dequeue then Enqueue to handle simultaneous operations with maximum throughput
36	  val deqState = state.dequeue(io.deqReady)
37	  val enqState = deqState.enqueue(io.enqData, io.enqValid)
38	
39	  state := Mux(io.flush, state.flush(), enqState)
40	  // Assert that the state is consistent after every cycle
41	  assert(state.invariant())
42	
43	  io.nEnqueued := state.count
44	  io.dataOut := state.peek(n)
45	}

1	# DMA Engine
2	
3	The DMA engine is a single-channel, linked-list descriptor DMA controller that
4	offloads bulk data movement from the CPU. It connects to the existing TileLink-UL
5	crossbar as both a host (master, for read/write transactions) and a device
6	(slave, for CPU programming via CSRs).
7	
8	Without a DMA engine, all memory transfers (loading model weights from SRAM/DDR
9	into TCMs, streaming peripheral data) must be performed by the CPU, stalling
10	execution.
11	
12	## Architecture
13	
14	The DMA engine has two TileLink-UL ports:
15	
16	- **Host port** (128-bit): Issues Get/PutFullData transactions on the crossbar to
17	  read from source addresses and write to destination addresses.
18	- **Device port** (32-bit): Accepts CSR read/write transactions from the CPU to
19	  program and monitor the DMA.
20	
21	The engine processes a linked list of descriptors stored in memory. Each
22	descriptor defines a single transfer: source address, destination address,
23	length, beat size, and optional peripheral flow control parameters. Descriptors
24	are chained via a `next_desc` pointer; a value of 0 signals end of chain.
25	
26	### Transfer Modes
27	
28	| Mode | Source Addr | Dest Addr | Use Case |
29	|------|-----------|----------|----------|
30	| Mem→Mem | Incrementing | Incrementing | SRAM↔DDR, SRAM→ITCM/DTCM |
31	| Mem→Periph | Incrementing | Fixed | SRAM→SPI TX FIFO |
32	| Periph→Mem | Fixed | Incrementing | I2C RX→SRAM |
33	
34	### Key Parameters
35	
36	- **Host port width**: 128-bit (matches crossbar common width)
37	- **Device port width**: 32-bit (CSR access, like GPIO/SPI)
38	- **Max transfer per descriptor**: 16 MB (24-bit length field)
39	- **Outstanding transactions**: 1 (single source ID, read-one-write-one)
40	- **Interrupt**: None for v1 (CPU polls STATUS register)
41	
42	## Register Map
43	
44	Base address: `0x40050000` (4 KB region, after I2C at `0x40040000`)
45	
46	| Offset | Name | Access | Bits | Description |
47	|--------|------|--------|------|-------------|
48	| `0x00` | CTRL | RW | [0] enable, [1] start (W1S, self-clearing), [2] abort | Control |
49	| `0x04` | STATUS | RO | [0] busy, [1] done, [2] error, [7:4] error_code | Status |
50	| `0x08` | DESC_ADDR | RW | [31:0] | Address of first descriptor in memory |
51	| `0x0C` | CUR_DESC | RO | [31:0] | Address of currently executing descriptor |
52	| `0x10` | XFER_REMAIN | RO | [23:0] | Bytes remaining in current transfer |
53	
54	### Programming Sequence
55	
56	```
57	1. Build descriptor chain in memory (SRAM or DDR)
58	2. Write DESC_ADDR with address of first descriptor
59	3. Write CTRL with enable=1, start=1
60	4. Poll STATUS.done until set
61	5. Check STATUS.error
62	```
63	
64	## Descriptor Format
65	
66	Descriptors are 32 bytes (two 128-bit TL-UL beats) and must be 32-byte aligned
67	in memory. The DMA fetches them via its host port.
68	
69	```
70	Offset  Field         Bits     Description
71	0x00    src_addr      [31:0]   Source address
72	0x04    dst_addr      [31:0]   Destination address
73	0x08    xfer_len      [23:0]   Transfer length in bytes
74	        xfer_width    [26:24]  Beat size: log2(bytes). 0=1B, 1=2B, 2=4B, 3=8B, 4=16B
75	        flags         [31:27]  [27] src_fixed, [28] dst_fixed, [29] poll_en, [30:31] reserved
76	0x0C    next_desc     [31:0]   Address of next descriptor (0 = end of chain)
77	0x10    poll_addr     [31:0]   Status register address to poll (0 = no polling)
78	0x14    poll_mask     [31:0]   Bitmask applied to polled value
79	0x18    poll_value    [31:0]   Expected value after masking
80	0x1C    reserved      [31:0]
81	```
82	
83	## Peripheral Flow Control
84	
85	Peripherals like SPI master expose status registers (TX Full, RX Empty flags).
86	The DMA uses **descriptor-level status polling** to pace transfers without
87	requiring any peripheral modifications.
88	
89	Each descriptor includes an optional `poll_addr` / `poll_mask` / `poll_value`
90	triplet. When configured (`poll_en` set and `poll_addr != 0`), the DMA reads
91	`poll_addr` before each data beat and waits until
92	`(read_data & poll_mask) == poll_value`.
93	
94	### Example: DMA → SPI TX
95	
96	```
97	Descriptor:
98	  src_addr   = 0x20000000  (SRAM buffer)
99	  dst_addr   = 0x40020008  (SPI TXDATA register)
100	  dst_fixed  = 1
101	  poll_addr  = 0x40020000  (SPI STATUS register)
102	  poll_mask  = 0x00000004  (bit 2 = TX Full)
103	  poll_value = 0x00000000  (wait until TX not full)
104	```
105	
106	The DMA reads SPI STATUS, checks `(status & 0x4) == 0`, and only then reads the
107	next source byte and writes it to TXDATA. This naturally paces the DMA to the
108	SPI clock rate.
109	
110	### Example: I2C RX → DMA
111	
112	```
113	Descriptor:
114	  src_addr   = 0x40040008  (I2C RXDATA register)
115	  dst_addr   = 0x20001000  (SRAM buffer)
116	  src_fixed  = 1
117	  poll_addr  = 0x40040000  (I2C STATUS register)
118	  poll_mask  = 0x00000002  (bit 1 = RX available)
119	  poll_value = 0x00000002  (wait until RX data ready)
120	```
121	
122	## State Machine
123	
124	```
125	IDLE ──[start]──► FETCH_DESC_0 ──[d.fire]──► FETCH_DESC_1 ──[d.fire]──► POLL_CHECK
126	  ▲                                                                          │
127	  │                                                          [no poll or match]
128	  │                                                                          ▼
129	  │                                                                   XFER_READ_REQ
130	  │                                                                          │
131	  │                  [poll_en &&                                         [a.fire]
132	  │                   mismatch]                                              ▼
133	  │                       │                                          XFER_READ_RESP
134	  │                  POLL_REQ ◄── POLL_RESP                                  │
135	  │                       │          ▲  │                                [d.fire]
136	  │                  [a.fire]        │  │                                     ▼
137	  │                       ▼          │  [match]                       XFER_WRITE_REQ
138	  │                  POLL_RESP ──────┘     │                                 │
139	  │                                        ▼                            [a.fire]
140	  │                                  XFER_READ_REQ                           ▼
141	  │                                                                   XFER_WRITE_RESP
142	  │                                                                          │
143	  │                                                               [d.fire, remaining>0]
144	  │                                                                     ──► POLL_CHECK
145	  │                                                               [d.fire, remaining==0,
146	  │                                                                next!=0]
147	  │                                                                     ──► FETCH_DESC_0
148	  │                                                               [d.fire, remaining==0,
149	  │                                                                next==0]
150	  │                                                                          │
151	  └────────────────────────── DONE ◄─────────────────────────────────────────┘
152	```
153	
154	### State Descriptions
155	
156	- **IDLE**: Waits for `CTRL.start`. Latches `DESC_ADDR`.
157	- **FETCH_DESC_0**: Issues TL-UL Get (128-bit) for descriptor bytes 0–15
158	  (src_addr, dst_addr, len/flags, next_desc).
159	- **FETCH_DESC_1**: Issues TL-UL Get (128-bit) for descriptor bytes 16–31
160	  (poll_addr, poll_mask, poll_value).
161	- **POLL_CHECK**: If `poll_en` is set and `poll_addr != 0`, go to POLL_REQ.
162	  Otherwise skip to XFER_READ_REQ.
163	- **POLL_REQ**: Issues TL-UL Get (32-bit) at `poll_addr`.
164	- **POLL_RESP**: Captures D channel data. If `(data & poll_mask) == poll_value`,
165	  proceed to XFER_READ_REQ. Otherwise loop back to POLL_REQ.
166	- **XFER_READ_REQ**: Issues TL-UL Get at current source address with configured
167	  beat size.
168	- **XFER_READ_RESP**: Captures D channel data into buffer register.
169	- **XFER_WRITE_REQ**: Issues TL-UL PutFullData with buffered data to dest
170	  address.
171	- **XFER_WRITE_RESP**: On D ack, updates addresses (unless fixed) and remaining
172	  length. If remaining > 0, loop to POLL_CHECK. If remaining == 0 and
173	  `next_desc != 0`, go to FETCH_DESC_0. Otherwise DONE.
174	- **DONE**: Sets `STATUS.done`, returns to IDLE.
175	
176	Abort from any state transitions to IDLE with error flag set.
177	TL-UL D channel error transitions to DONE with error code.
178	
179	## TileLink Host Interface
180	
181	Single 128-bit TL-UL master port. Generates:
182	
183	- **Get** (read): opcode=4, size=`xfer_width`, address=`src_addr`, mask=all-ones
184	  for size
185	- **PutFullData** (write): opcode=0, size=`xfer_width`, address=`dst_addr`,
186	  data=buffer
187	- **Poll Get**: opcode=4, size=2 (32-bit), address=`poll_addr`
188	- **Descriptor Get**: opcode=4, size=4 (16 bytes), address=`desc_addr` /
189	  `desc_addr+16`
190	
191	Source ID always 0 (single outstanding).
192	
193	The host A channel is shared between descriptor fetch, poll reads, data reads,
194	and data writes. The FSM drives a mux selecting the appropriate
195	opcode/address/data/size based on current state.
196	
197	## TileLink Device Interface
198	
199	Follows the GPIO pattern (`hdl/chisel/src/bus/GPIO.scala`):
200	
201	- `tl_a.ready := !tl_d_valid`
202	- On `tl_a.fire`: decode `address[11:0]`, read/write CSRs
203	- Start bit triggers state machine kick
204	
205	## Crossbar Integration
206	
207	### Address Map
208	
209	The DMA occupies `0x40050000–0x40050FFF` (4 KB), after I2C at `0x40040000`.
210	
211	### Host Connectivity
212	
213	The DMA host port connects to all memory and peripheral devices it may need to
214	access:
215	
216	```
217	"dma" -> Seq("sram", "coralnpu_device", "rom", "ddr_ctrl", "ddr_mem",
218	             "spi_master", "gpio", "i2c_master", "uart0", "uart1")
219	```
220	
221	The CPU must also be able to program the DMA:
222	
223	```
224	"coralnpu_core" -> Seq(...existing..., "dma")
225	```
226	
227	## Implementation
228	
229	Single new file: `hdl/chisel/src/bus/DmaEngine.scala`
230	
231	Configuration changes in:
232	- `hdl/chisel/src/soc/CrossbarConfig.scala` — host, device, address range,
233	  connections
234	- `hdl/chisel/src/soc/SoCChiselConfig.scala` — `DmaParameters`, module config
235	- `hdl/chisel/src/soc/CoralNPUChiselSubsystem.scala` — instantiation case
236	
237	### Module IO
238	
239	```scala
240	class DmaEngine(hostParams: Parameters, deviceParams: Parameters) extends Module {
241	  val hostTlulP = new TLULParameters(hostParams)
242	  val deviceTlulP = new TLULParameters(deviceParams)
243	  val io = IO(new Bundle {
244	    val tl_host   = new OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device(hostTlulP)
245	    val tl_device = Flipped(new OpenTitanTileLink.Host2Device(deviceTlulP))
246	  })
247	}
248	```
249	
250	### Internal Structure
251	
252	- **CSR register file**: Regs for CTRL, STATUS, DESC_ADDR, following GPIO pattern
253	- **Descriptor latch**: Registers for all descriptor fields, loaded during FETCH
254	  states
255	- **Data buffer**: 128-bit register for read-then-write pipeline
256	- **Address counters**: Current src/dst addresses, remaining byte count
257	- **FSM**: ChiselEnum with states listed above
258	- **Integrity**: `RequestIntegrityGen` for host A channel,
259	  `ResponseIntegrityGen` for device D channel
260

1	# CoralNPU Dispatch Rules
2	
3	We want to dispatch as many instructions as possible in the CoralNPU core. The
4	following describes the general rules we use to determine which instructions can
5	be dispatcted.
6	
7	## In-order
8	
9	CoralNPU is an in-order core. In at instruction at address n cannot be dispatched,
10	n+4 is also not considered for dispatch.
11	
12	## Hazard Handling
13	
14	CoralNPU uses scoreboarding to track dependencies across instructions. This
15	prevents RAW and WAW data hazards. All execution units read their operands from
16	the register file the cycle after the instructions are dispatched. Therefore,
17	WAR hazard never occurs.
18	
19	## Execution Unit Constraints
20	
21	There are a limited number of execution units to service instructions. While
22	there are enough Alu and Bru units to service each lane, CoralNPU contains only
23	1 Mlu. Therefore, we restrict the number of multiply instructions per-cycle to
24	a single instruction. Simiarily, non-pipelined execution units (ie. Dvu) may
25	exert backpressure to prevent an instruction from being dispatched while it is
26	busy.
27	
28	Memory today is limited to dispatching one instruction per cycle.
29	
30	## Control Flow
31	
32	Conservatively, CoralNPU will not dispatch past the following jump instructions:
33	`jal`, `jalr`, `ebreak`, `ecall`, `mret`, `wfi`.
34	
35	## Special Instructions
36	
37	Instructions that can affect the core state beyond the PC/RegisterFile are
38	limited to executing out of the first slot. They are also typically treated as
39	jump control flow instructions, so no other instructions should be dispatched in
40	the same cycle as these. These instructions are: `csrrw`, `csrrs`, `csrrc`
41	`ebreak`, `ecall`, `mret`, `fence`, `fenci` and `wfi`.

# Coral NPU Repository Comprehensive Analysis

## 1. Overview & Top-Level Structure

Coral NPU is a Google open-source RISC-V based ML accelerator (`rv32imf_zve32x_zicsr_zifencei_zbb`). The codebase is a Bazel-managed monorepo. **All RTL/firmware sources have been removed; only test infrastructure, BUILD files, documentation, and a couple of supporting C++ DPI files remain.**

### Top-Level Directories (`/app/`)
| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/app/.bazelrc`, `/app/.bazelversion`, `/app/WORKSPACE`, `/app/BUILD.bazel` | Bazel workspace config |
| `/app/README.md`, `/app/CONTRIBUTING.md`, `/app/LICENSE` | Project metadata |
| `/app/doc/` | Architecture & microarch documentation |
| `/app/hdl/` | Hardware description (Chisel + Verilog) — sources removed |
| `/app/tests/` | Verilator C++ TBs, cocotb Python+SV tests |
| `/app/sw/` | NPU-targeted software/sim utilities |
| `/app/fpga/` | FPGA build harness (Verilator/Nexus/IP cores) |
| `/app/examples/` | Sample programs (`hello_world_add_floats.cc`, etc.) |
| `/app/coralnpu_test_utils/` | Python test interface libraries |
| `/app/lib/`, `/app/utils/`, `/app/rules/`, `/app/toolchain/`, `/app/third_party/`, `/app/platforms/` | Build glue |
| `/app/hw_sim/`, `/app/run_isp_cam_sim.sh`, `/app/jtag-sim.cfg` | Simulator runners |

## 2. Key Documentation

### `/app/README.md`
- Coral NPU = NPU/AI accelerator, RV32IMF + Zve32x.
- **Features**: 4-stage pipeline; in-order dispatch / out-of-order retire; 4-way scalar, 2-way vector dispatch; 128-bit SIMD (256-bit future); 8 KB ITCM + 32 KB DTCM single-cycle SRAMs; AXI4 master/slave.
- Quick-start commands: `bazel run //tests/cocotb:core_mini_axi_sim_cocotb`, build `//examples:coralnpu_v2_hello_world_add_floats`, build `//tests/verilator_sim:core_mini_axi_sim`.

### `/app/doc/overview.md`
- Three processor components (matrix, vector/SIMD, scalar) fused around a quantized outer-product MAC engine (256 MACs/cycle).
- Custom RV32IM frontend; the C-extension encoding is reclaimed for SIMD register indices and stripmining.
- Backwards branches taken / forwards not-taken policy in fetch.
- 31 scalar regs, 64 vector regs (256-bit), 8x8x32 accumulator.
- Stripmining: a single dispatch like `vadd v0` produces 4 issues `vadd v0..v3` to backend.
- L1Icache: 8 KB, 4-way associative, 256-bit blocks. L1Dcache: 16 KB, 4-way, dual 8 KB banks; flushing stalls until completion.

### `/app/doc/integration_guide.md`
- Describes the AXI integration variant (`core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog`).
- Module ports: `clk`, `reset`, `s_axi`, `m_axi`, `irqn`, `wfi`, `debug`, `halted`, `fault`.
- AXI master/slave channel signal semantics.
- Memory map: ITCM `0x0000–0x1FFF` (8 kB), DTCM `0x10000–0x17FFF` (32 kB), CSR `0x30000+`.
- External CSRs: `RESET_CONTROL` (`0x0`, RESET[0], CLOCK_GATE[1]), `PC_START` (`0x4`), `STATUS` (`0x8`, HALTED[0], FAULT[1]).
- Boot sequence: load ITCM, write PC_START, release clock gate, release reset, monitor STATUS.
- Synchronous reset strategy.

### `/app/doc/microarch/microarch.md`
- 3-stage in-order pipeline (Fetch → Decode/Dispatch → Execute/Writeback).
- Dispatches up to 4 instructions/cycle with scoreboard/interlock.
- Latencies: Alu/Csr/Bru = 1, Mlu = 2, Dvu = variable, Lsu = 2+.

### `/app/doc/microarch/dispatch.md`
- In-order; if instr at addr n cannot dispatch, n+4 isn't either.
- Scoreboarding for RAW/WAW; WAR avoided via day-after read.
- Single Mlu, non-pipelined Dvu.
- Conservative jump barrier: `jal/jalr/ebreak/ecall/mret/wfi`.
- `csrrw/csrrs/csrrc/ebreak/ecall/mret/fence/fenci/wfi` are slot-0 only.

### `/app/doc/microarch/lsu.md`
- Per-slot table managing single LSU operation; states Idle → VectorUpdate → TransferMemory → Writeback.
- Three buses: `ibus` (read-only 128-bit), `dbus` (TCM, 128-bit + 16-bit wmask), `ebus` (external, has fault sub-bundle: valid/write/addr/epc).
- `rvv2lsu`/`lsu2rvv` interfaces wired to vector regfile (idx + vregfile + mask, 128-bit data).

### `/app/doc/microarch/mlu.md`
- 4 per-lane req inputs (op, addr, valid, ready, rs1/rs2 valid+data).
- Single rd output (valid, addr 5-bit, data 32-bit, ready).
- 3 stages: dispatch → compute → writeback.

### `/app/doc/peripherals/dma.md`
- DMA engine spec: dual TLUL ports (host 128-bit, device 32-bit). Located in `hdl/chisel/src/bus/DmaEngine.scala`.
- Base 0x40050000. Registers: CTRL/STATUS/DESC_ADDR/CUR_DESC/XFER_REMAIN.
- 32-byte descriptor format; FSM IDLE→FETCH_DESC_0/1→POLL_CHECK→XFER_READ/WRITE→DONE.
- Modes: mem→mem, mem→peripheral, peripheral→mem; up to 16 MB transfer.

Other docs: `/app/doc/microarch/debug.md`, `/app/doc/sw/dma.md`, `/app/doc/simulation.md`, `/app/doc/tutorials/{writing_coralnpu_programs,npusim_mobilenet_tutorial}.md`.

`core_mini_axi_tb.h` shows the expected DUT signal hierarchy:
- AXI master: `AXISignals<axi2AddrBits, lsuDataBits, axi2IdBits, 8 (axLEN), 1 (axLOCK), 0,0,0,0,0>`.
- DUT control: `io_halted`, `io_fault`, `io_wfi`, `io_irq`, `io_timer_irq`, `io_software_irq`, `io_te`, `io_boot_addr` (32 bits).
- `DebugIO` carries 4 fetch lanes (en/addr_/inst_), DBus debug, dispatch_{0..3}_inst{Fire,Addr,Inst}, regfile writeAddr_{0..3} + writeData_{0..5}, conditionally Float writeAddr/writeData (when KP_enableFloat), retirement-buffer arrays sized by `KP_retirementBufferSize`/`KP_retirementBufferIdxWidth`. With RVV: vec writes (8 per slot) of width `KP_rvvVlen`.
- `DebugModuleIO`: `req_{valid,ready,bits.{address,data,op}}`, `rsp_{valid,ready,bits.{data,op}}`.
- CSR base address: 0x30000 (default) or 0x200000 (highmem).
- xbar 2:1 TLM mux for tohost/fromhost semihosting.

C++ symbol expectations from verilator-generated headers: `KP_axi2AddrBits`, `KP_lsuDataBits`, `KP_axi2IdBits`, `KP_enableFloat`, `KP_enableRvv`, `KP_rvvVlen`, `KP_retirementBufferSize`, `KP_retirementBufferIdxWidth` — confirms the chisel emit produces `*_parameters.h`.

To produce a build that satisfies the existing tests, the missing Chisel + SystemVerilog sources must be authored such that:

- All `chisel_test` targets in `/app/hdl/chisel/src/{common,bus,coralnpu,peripherals}/BUILD` build & run.
- `chisel_cc_library` emit objects (e.g., `coralnpu.EmitCore`, `bus.EmitAxi2TLUL`, `coralnpu.soc.CoralNPUXbarEmitter`) generate SystemVerilog that Verilator can compile.
- Cocotb test suites (`core_mini_axi_sim_cocotb`, `rvv_core_mini_axi_sim_cocotb`, `tlul_*`, `coralnpu_xbar_cocotb`, `coralnpu_chisel_subsystem_cocotb`, `dma_integration_cocotb`, `gpio_integration_cocotb`, `spi_master_cocotb`) link against the verilator models and exercise the DUT through `coralnpu_test_utils.core_mini_axi_interface.CoreMiniAxiInterface`, `TileLinkULInterface`, `axi_slave`, `spi_master`, etc.
- Verilator C++ binaries (`core_mini_axi_sim`, `rvv_core_mini_axi_sim`, etc.) link against the Chisel-emitted models including `*_parameters.h`.
